7d(1).fact: Proper bourse etiquette requires asking permission before touching any specimen and holding unslabbed coins solely by their rims to prevent corrosion from skin oils.
7d(1).misconception: Dealers at coin shows permit attendees to pick up bare coins directly by their obverse and reverse faces to inspect fine details.
7d(1).pamphlet_summary: Visiting a commercial coin bourse allows collectors to observe trading etiquette, inspect dealer inventories, and examine certified coins displayed under specialized lighting. Scouts should always ask permission before handling items and hold raw pieces strictly by their edges (p. 45).
7d(1).socratic_question: When you approach a dealer table at a coin show, why is it necessary to ask before touching a coin and hold it only by its outer rim?

7d(2).fact: Local coin clubs welcome hobbyists of all ages and focus primarily on educational presentations, collector fellowship, and modest member auctions.
7d(2).misconception: Coin club meetings are formal sales events restricted to professional dealers and adults with large financial investments.
7d(2).pamphlet_summary: Local numismatic clubs offer educational presentations, member auctions, and show-and-tell sessions that introduce collectors to specialized collecting fields. Participating in a meeting gives Scouts direct access to knowledgeable mentors who share preservation advice and grading insights (p. 44).
7d(2).socratic_question: How can attending a local coin club meeting help you discover new collecting specialties that you might never encounter on your own?

7d(3).fact: Circulating coins are struck once at high speed on standard presses, whereas proof coins are individually fed and struck multiple times at lower speeds with specially polished dies.
7d(3).misconception: All United States Mint facilities strike both circulating coins and collector proof sets on identical high-speed production presses.
7d(3).pamphlet_summary: Touring an active production facility in Philadelphia or Denver shows how blank metal coils are punched into planchets, upset with raised rims, and struck by coining presses. Visitors observe high-speed automated sorting, proof striking, and stringent quality control inspections firsthand (p. 47).
7d(3).socratic_question: What mechanical steps must a flat metal disk undergo inside a mint facility before it becomes a finished circulating coin?

7d(4).fact: A virtual tour must explore curated educational exhibits from recognized institutions such as the Smithsonian National Numismatic Collection or the American Numismatic Association Money Museum.
7d(4).misconception: Browsing coin sales websites or commercial auction listings satisfies the requirement for an approved virtual museum tour.
7d(4).pamphlet_summary: Online museum galleries provide interactive access to high-resolution images of legendary numismatic rarities, ancient currency, and historic dies that are not on physical display. Scouts must secure parent permission and counselor approval before examining curated digital collections from institutions like the Smithsonian or the American Numismatic Association (p. 48).
7d(4).socratic_question: What makes a curated museum exhibit online different from browsing commercial auction listings when studying the historical significance of money?
